usage: The textbook collocation; the thing studied takes 을/를, never 에.
Pairs naturally with 원인 (cause) and 결과 (result) in reports.
Adverb 자세히 (in detail) or 철저히 (thoroughly) intensifies the act.
The bare noun 분석 plus 결과 — what you present after the verb's work is done.
examples: 이 표를 분석해요
I analyze this chart
Simplest object + 를 + 분석하다 frame; note the 하다→해요 contraction.
결과를 분석한 후에 다시 이야기해요
Let's talk again after analyzing the results
분석한 후에 = 'after analyzing' shows the past-modifier -ㄴ before 후에.
이 보고서는 시장 흐름을 아주 자세히 분석했어요
This report analyzed the market trend in great detail
Real report register: 자세히 + 분석했어요, the workhorse academic past tense.
nuance: 분석하다 means to analyze — to break a whole down into its parts (分 'divide' + 析 'split apart') so you can understand how it works: data, a cause, a problem, or a text. The hanja itself pictures cutting something open, which is why it always implies methodical dissection, not a casual glance. As a 하다 verb it must contract to 분석해요 (never 분석하요), and the object always takes 을/를. The pitfall for English speakers is register: in English you 'analyze' anything, but 분석하다 sounds clinical and academic, so for everyday 'let me look into it' Koreans reach for 살펴보다 (look over) or 알아보다 (check / find out). The near-synonym to watch is 분석하다 vs 분류하다: 분석하다 takes one thing apart to study it, while 분류하다 sorts many things into groups — analyzing a single survey vs classifying responses by age.

mistakes: Writing 분석하요 — 하다 never stays as 하 before 요; it always contracts to 분석해요.
Saying 데이터에 분석해요. The thing analyzed is a direct object, so it must be 데이터를 분석해요.
Using 분석하다 for a quick everyday peek; for 'let me just look into it' 살펴볼게요 or 알아볼게요 sounds far more natural.

usage: Standard workplace frame: object + 를 + 평가하다 for appraisals.
to think highly of / rate highly
Needs the adverb 높게 (highly), not the adjective 높은.
Opposite of 높게; 낮게 평가하다 = to rate something below its worth.
공정하게 (fairly) is the buzzword for grading and hiring contexts.
examples: 그 영화를 어떻게 평가해요?
How do you rate that movie?
어떻게 평가해요? is the everyday way to ask for someone's assessment.
선생님이 학생들의 발표를 평가했어요
The teacher evaluated the students' presentations
Grading context; 발표를 평가했어요 with the plain past.
사람을 겉모습으로만 평가하지 마세요
Don't judge people only by their appearance
겉모습으로만 = 'by appearance alone'; 으로 marks the basis of judgment.
nuance: 평가하다 means to evaluate, assess, or rate the value of something — work, performance, art, or even a person (評 'judge/criticize' + 價 'price/value', literally 'to price-judge'). That 價 'value' core is why it feels measured and official, the word on report cards, performance reviews, and product reviews. As a 하다 verb it contracts to 평가해요. With 높게/좋게 평가하다 it means 'to think highly of', and 낮게 평가하다 means 'to underrate' — note these always need the ADVERB (높게), a spot English speakers trip on by reaching for 높은. The synonym line to hold is 평가하다 vs 판단하다: 평가하다 weighs worth on a scale (high/low, good/bad), while 판단하다 reaches a yes/no decision about a situation. Because 평가하다 can sound like you are sitting in judgment, Koreans soften it when appraising people directly, or switch to 판단하다.

mistakes: Writing 평가하요 instead of the contracted 평가해요.
Saying 높은 평가해요 for 'rate highly' — it must be the adverb: 높게 평가해요.
Using 평가하다 to mean 'judge a person harshly' in casual talk; it sounds cold, so 판단하다 or a softened phrasing fits better.

usage: Object + 를 + 증명하다 for establishing something is true.
Everyday bureaucratic use; relates to the noun 증명서 (certificate).
A set legal collocation; 결백 (innocence) habitually pairs with this verb.
증명해 보이다 adds 'show that you can' — proving to convince doubters.
examples: 이 자료가 그 사실을 증명해 줘요
This material proves that fact
증명해 주다 = 'serves as proof'; -아/어 주다 frames it as doing a favor.
그는 끝까지 자신의 결백을 증명했어요
He proved his innocence to the end
결백을 증명했어요 — the courtroom collocation in the plain past.
그걸 어떻게 증명할 수 있어요?
How can you prove that?
증명할 수 있어요 is the 'can' form, challenging someone to back a claim.
nuance: 증명하다 means to prove or demonstrate that something is true with evidence or logic — a fact, one's innocence, identity, or a theorem (證 'evidence/testimony' + 明 'make clear', literally 'make clear through evidence'). That 證 'evidence' root is the whole point: you cannot 증명하다 by merely asserting; you need proof, which is also why the noun 증명서 means an official certificate (재직증명서 = proof of employment). As a 하다 verb it contracts to 증명해요. The trap for English speakers is the verb pair 증명하다 vs 설명하다: in English 'prove' and 'explain' feel close, but 설명하다 just makes something understandable, while 증명하다 establishes it as TRUE. Likewise keep it apart from 보여주다 (to show / display): 보여주다 puts something in view; 증명하다 wins an argument with it.

As a 하다 verb it contracts to 증명해요.

mistakes: Writing 증명하요 instead of the contracted 증명해요.
Using 증명하다 when you only mean 'make clear' — that is 설명하다 (explain); 증명하다 demands evidence.
Confusing it with 보여주다 (to show): you 보여주다 a photo, but you 증명하다 the truth the photo supports.

usage: Object + 를 + 주장하다 = to push a position you hold.
The quotation frame -(ㄴ/는)다고 주장하다 reports the claimed content.
끝까지 (to the end) underscores the stubborn 'won't back down' nuance.
근거 없이 (without basis) flags an unsupported, weak assertion.
examples: 저는 제가 옳다고 주장해요
I argue that I'm right
-다고 주장하다 reports your own claim; 옳다고 from 옳다 (be right).
전문가들은 그 방법이 위험하다고 주장해요
Experts argue that the method is dangerous
위험하다고 — adjective + -다고, the news/academic reporting frame.
근거 없이 주장하지 마세요
Don't make claims without evidence
근거 없이 + 주장하지 마세요 warns against unsupported insistence.
nuance: 주장하다 means to argue, insist on, or claim a position you strongly believe and want others to accept (主 'main/master' + 張 'stretch/spread out', literally 'stretch out as one's main point'). That 主 'master/own' nuance is why it always carries personal conviction — you are pushing YOUR stance, not neutrally reporting. As a 하다 verb it contracts to 주장해요, and to report the content you claim you use the quotation frame -(ㄴ/는)다고 주장하다. The pitfall is 주장하다 vs 말하다: English speakers translate 'I said that...' with 주장하다, but 말하다 is neutral telling while 주장하다 implies you are taking a contested stand and defending it. Bonus: the noun 주장 also means 'team captain' in sports (the one who 'masters/leads'), so judge it by context.

structuredNuance.t: To argue, insist on, or claim a position you strongly believe and want others to accept. It always carries personal conviction — you are pushing YOUR stance, not neutrally reporting. Bonus: the noun 주장 also means 'team captain' in sports (the one who 'masters/leads'), so judge it by context.
主 'main/master' + 張 'stretch/spread out', literally 'stretch out as one's main point'. That 主 'master/own' nuance is the source of its personal conviction.
As a 하다 verb it contracts to 주장해요, and to report the content you claim you use the quotation frame -(ㄴ/는)다고 주장하다.
주장하다 vs 말하다: 말하다 is neutral telling, while 주장하다 implies you are taking a contested stand and defending it.
English speakers translate 'I said that...' with 주장하다, but a neutral 'I said' is 말하다 — reach for 주장하다 only when you are insisting on a contested point.

mistakes: Writing 주장하요 instead of the contracted 주장해요.
Using 주장하다 for a neutral 'I said' — that is 말하다; 주장하다 implies you are insisting on a contested point.
Dropping the quotation marker: claim THAT something is so needs -다고 주장하다, e.g. 위험하다고 주장하다, not 위험하다 주장하다.

usage: The flagship collocation; 중요성 (importance) is the default object.
다시 한번 (one more time) — speaker's set phrase for driving a point home.
특히 (especially) singles out one point above the rest.
거듭 (over and over) is the formal written cousin of 다시 한번.
examples: 이 점을 특히 강조하고 싶어요
I especially want to emphasize this point
이 점 (this point) + 강조하고 싶어요 — the speaker spotlighting one item.
선생님은 예습의 중요성을 강조했어요
The teacher emphasized the importance of preparation
예습의 중요성을 강조했어요, the classic lecture-hall past tense.
그분은 항상 정직을 강조하세요
That person always emphasizes honesty
강조하세요 adds the honorific -시-; 정직 (honesty) as the value stressed.
nuance: 강조하다 means to emphasize, stress, or underline that something matters (強 'strong' + 調 'tone/tune', literally 'to set a strong tone'). That 強 'strong' element is why the word belongs to lectures, presentations, and persuasive writing — you are raising the volume on one point. As a 하다 verb it contracts to 강조해요, and the point stressed takes 을/를 (중요성을 강조하다), a spot where English speakers wrongly slip in 에. The synonym boundary to keep is 강조하다 vs 주장하다: 강조하다 turns up the weight of a point everyone may already accept ('this really matters'), whereas 주장하다 pushes a contested CLAIM others might reject. So a teacher 강조한다 that review is important, but a debater 주장한다 that a policy is wrong.

structuredNuance.t: To emphasize, stress, or underline that something matters. It belongs to lectures, presentations, and persuasive writing — you are raising the volume on one point.
強 'strong' + 調 'tone/tune', literally 'to set a strong tone'. That 強 'strong' element is why it fits anywhere you turn up the weight on a point.
As a 하다 verb it contracts to 강조해요, and the point stressed takes 을/를 (중요성을 강조하다), a spot where English speakers wrongly slip in 에.

강조하다 vs 주장하다: 강조하다 turns up the weight of a point everyone may already accept ('this really matters'), whereas 주장하다 pushes a contested CLAIM others might reject. So a teacher 강조한다 that review is important, but a debater 주장한다 that a policy is wrong.

mistakes: Writing 강조하요 instead of the contracted 강조해요.
Using 에 for the point emphasized — say 중요성을 강조해요, not 중요성에 강조해요.
Reaching for 강조하다 when you mean to push a debatable claim; that is 주장하다, while 강조하다 just amplifies a point.

usage: Object + 를 + 제안하다 = to put forward a plan or idea.
The frame -자고 제안하다 reports a suggestion to act jointly.
대안 (alternative) is a stock business object for this verb.
Softer indirect frame; reports a 'how about ~?' suggestion.
examples: 그가 좋은 아이디어를 제안했어요
He proposed a good idea
아이디어를 제안했어요 — straightforward object in a work setting.
같이 점심을 먹자고 제안했어요
I suggested we eat lunch together
먹자고 제안했어요 shows -자고 reporting a shared suggestion.
더 나은 해결책을 제안해 주세요
Please propose a better solution
해결책 (solution) + 제안해 주세요, the polite request form.
nuance: 제안하다 means to propose or put forward a plan, idea, or course of action, usually in a formal or business setting (提 'lift/raise up' + 案 'plan/proposal', literally 'to raise a proposal'). The 提 'raise up' image fits a meeting where you formally table an idea. As a 하다 verb it contracts to 제안해요; to suggest doing something together you attach the propositive quotation -자고 제안하다 (먹자고 제안하다). The pitfall is 제안하다 vs 추천하다: English 'suggest' blurs them, but 제안하다 floats a NEW plan or course of action ('let's try this approach'), while 추천하다 recommends a specific known thing as good ('try this restaurant'). Because 제안하다 sounds formal, in casual chat Koreans drop it for V-자 or V-는 게 어때요?.

mistakes: Writing 제안하요 instead of the contracted 제안해요.
Using 제안하다 to recommend a specific item (a film, a shop) — that is 추천하다; 제안하다 is for proposing a plan or action.
Forgetting the propositive marker for joint suggestions: 'let's meet' reported is 만나자고 제안하다, not 만나 제안하다.

usage: Critical particle: the thing opposed takes 에, NOT 을/를.
계획에 반대하다 — same 에 pattern in a business setting.
강력히 (forcefully) is the news-headline intensifier for firm opposition.
The bare noun 반대 modifies 의견 to name the opposite stance.
examples: 저는 그 의견에 반대하지 않아요
I don't oppose that opinion
에 반대하다 in the negative; 그 의견에 marks what you're against.
부모님이 그 결혼에 반대하셨어요
My parents opposed the marriage
결혼에 반대하셨어요 with honorific -시-; the classic family-drama line.
왜 그 계획에 반대하세요?
Why do you oppose the plan?
Asking someone's reason; 계획에 반대하세요 keeps the 에 particle.
nuance: 반대하다 means to oppose, object to, or be against something (反 'reverse/anti' + 對 'face/oppose', literally 'to face in the opposite direction'). The single most important thing for intermediate learners is the PARTICLE: the thing you oppose takes 에, never 을/를 — 의견에 반대하다, 계획에 반대하다. English 'oppose X' treats X as a direct object, so learners overwhelmingly write 의견을 반대해요, which is wrong. As a 하다 verb it contracts to 반대해요. Its clean antonym is 찬성하다 (to be in favor), which shares the same 에 frame. Keep it apart from 거부하다 (to refuse): 반대하다 is taking a stance against an idea in discussion, while 거부하다 is actively turning down a concrete request or offer.

反 'reverse/anti' + 對 'face/oppose', literally 'to face in the opposite direction'.

Writing 반대하요 instead of the contracted 반대해요.
Mixing it with 거부하다 (refuse a request); 반대하다 is opposing a view, 거부하다 is rejecting a concrete offer.

english: to agree / to be in favor
usage: to be in favor of an opinion
Like 반대하다, it takes 에: the thing supported is 에 찬성하다.
제안에 찬성하다 — the 에 frame in a meeting or vote.
to strongly support / be all for it
Bare noun 찬성 modifies 의견 to name the 'in favor' position in a debate.
examples: 저는 그 계획에 찬성해요
I'm in favor of the plan
계획에 찬성해요 in a discussion; note the 에, parallel to 반대하다.
대부분의 사람들이 그 의견에 찬성했어요
Most people agreed with that opinion
Reporting a vote or poll result; 의견에 찬성했어요.
찬성하면 손을 들어 주세요
If you agree, please raise your hand
찬성하면 = 'if in favor', the show-of-hands voting context.
nuance: 찬성하다 means to agree with, approve of, or be in favor of a proposal or opinion, especially in a vote or formal discussion (贊 'approve/assist' + 成 'accomplish', literally 'to approve and help bring about'). Like its antonym 반대하다, the thing you support takes 에 — 의견에 찬성하다 — and English speakers must resist writing 의견을 찬성해요. As a 하다 verb it contracts to 찬성해요. The key synonym contrast is 찬성하다 vs 동의하다: 찬성하다 is voting YES on a proposal or motion ('all in favor'), while 동의하다 is agreeing with a person's point or feeling in conversation. For 'I agree with you' in everyday talk, Koreans say 동의해요 or simply 맞아요, not 찬성해요, which would sound like a formal vote.

贊 'approve/assist' + 成 'accomplish', literally 'to approve and help bring about'.
Like its antonym 반대하다, the thing you support takes 에 — 의견에 찬성하다 — and English speakers must resist writing 의견을 찬성해요. As a 하다 verb it contracts to 찬성해요.

Writing 찬성하요 instead of the contracted 찬성해요.
Using 찬성하다 for 'I agree with you' in chat; that is 동의해요 or 맞아요 — 찬성하다 implies a formal vote on a motion.

usage: Object + 를 + 거부하다 = to turn down firmly. Note: 을/를, unlike 반대하다's 에.
요청 (request) and 요구 (demand) are the stock objects.
단호히 (resolutely) matches the verb's already-firm tone.
거부하다 on an action noun = a principled boycott or walk-out.
examples: 그는 인터뷰를 거부했어요
He refused the interview
인터뷰를 거부했어요 — a flat, firm refusal; object takes 를.
회사가 그의 요구를 단호히 거부했어요
The company flatly rejected his demands
요구를 단호히 거부했어요, the news-report register for firm rejection.
정당한 요청을 거부하지 마세요
Don't refuse a legitimate request
정당한 (legitimate) + 거부하지 마세요 urges against unfair refusal.
nuance: 거부하다 means to refuse, reject, or decline firmly — a proposal, request, demand, or order (拒 'ward off/resist' + 否 'no/deny', literally 'to ward off with a no'). Those hanja 'resist' + 'deny' make it strong and confrontational, the word for turning something down outright, often on principle. As a 하다 verb it contracts to 거부해요, and unlike 반대하다 the object takes 을/를 (요청을 거부하다). The pitfall is the synonym pair 거부하다 vs 거절하다: 거절하다 is the polite, softer 'decline' you use for an invitation or kind offer you'd rather not accept (제안을 정중히 거절했어요), whereas 거부하다 is a blunt, principled REFUSAL — a company 거부하다 demands, a witness 거부하다 to testify. Using 거부하다 when a friend invites you to dinner sounds harshly cold.

mistakes: Writing 거부하요 instead of the contracted 거부해요.
Using 에 like with 반대하다 — 거부하다 takes a direct object: 요청을 거부해요, not 요청에 거부해요.
Using 거부하다 to politely turn down an invitation; that blunt tone offends — use 거절하다 for soft declines.

usage: Object + 를 + 제공하다; 정보 and 서비스 are the top objects.
The recipient takes 에게/한테, the thing given takes 을/를.
무료로 (for free) is the marketing-notice staple with this verb.
Set business collocation seen on signs and contracts everywhere.
examples: 이 호텔은 무료 아침 식사를 제공해요
This hotel provides free breakfast
Service context; 아침 식사를 제공해요 on a hotel notice.
회사가 직원들에게 점심을 제공했어요
The company provided lunch to the employees
직원들에게 ... 점심을 제공했어요 shows the 에게 recipient frame.
자세한 정보를 제공해 주세요
Please provide detailed information
정보를 제공해 주세요, the polite request a customer makes.
nuance: 제공하다 means to provide, supply, or furnish something — information, services, food, resources — typically by an organization or in a formal context (提 'offer/raise up' + 供 'supply/offer', two 'give' hanja stacked for an official 'furnish'). Because both characters mean offering, the word feels institutional, the verb on hotel signs, contracts, and corporate notices. As a 하다 verb it contracts to 제공해요; the recipient takes 에게/한테 and the thing provided takes 을/를. The pitfall is register, not grammar: 제공하다 vs 주다. English 'give/provide' covers both, but 주다 is the warm everyday 'give' between people (친구가 선물을 줬어요), while 제공하다 is what a company or service does. Saying a friend 제공했어요 a gift sounds like a press release; use 줬어요.

mistakes: Writing 제공하요 instead of the contracted 제공해요.
Marking the recipient with 을/를 — it takes 에게/한테: 직원들에게 점심을 제공했어요.
Using 제공하다 for a friend giving you something; that stiff, corporate tone calls for 주다 instead.

usage: Active frame: the whole includes the part, which takes 을/를.
The passive partner 포함되다 + -어 있다 describes the included state.
A fixed set phrase that tacks 'including ~' onto a count or list.
비용/배송비 (cost/shipping) are everyday objects on price listings.
examples: 이 가격은 배송비를 포함해요
This price includes the shipping fee
Active 포함하다: 가격(whole) includes 배송비(part), object takes 를.
모든 비용이 포함되어 있어요
All costs are included
Passive 포함되어 있어요 — the part is the subject and takes 이/가.
저를 포함해서 다섯 명이에요
Including me, there are five people
저를 포함해서 = 'including me', the handy counting set phrase.
nuance: 포함하다 means to include or contain something inside a larger whole (包 'wrap/envelop' + 含 'hold in the mouth/contain', literally 'to wrap and hold within'). The 'wrap around' image is why the bigger thing 포함하다 the smaller part. As a 하다 verb it contracts to 포함해요. The single most useful thing to learn is its passive partner 포함되다 (to be included), which flips the roles: active 가격이 세금을 포함해요 (price includes tax, part = object 을/를) vs passive 세금이 가격에 포함돼요 / 포함되어 있어요 (tax is included, part = subject 이/가). English speakers blur these and say 세금이 포함해요, which is wrong — if tax is the one being included, it must be the passive 포함되다. Also memorize the frozen phrase N을/를 포함해(서) = 'including N'.

Saying 세금이 포함해요 — if the part is the subject, use the passive: 세금이 포함되어 있어요.

usage: The two compared join with 와/과 (or 하고), the whole takes 를.
진짜/가짜 (real/fake) is the textbook pair for this verb.
to be hard to tell apart
구별하기 + 어렵다 = 'hard to distinguish', the natural complaint frame.
옳고 그름 (right and wrong) — a fixed moral-judgment collocation.
examples: 이 둘은 어떻게 구별해요?
How do you tell these two apart?
Asking the trick for two look-alikes; 이 둘은 ... 구별해요?
저는 쌍둥이를 잘 구별하지 못해요
I can't tell the twins apart well
구별하지 못해요 = the 'unable to' negative for lacking the skill.
어른은 옳고 그름을 구별할 줄 알아야 해요
An adult should know how to tell right from wrong
구별할 줄 알다 = 'know how to distinguish', a maturity expectation.
nuance: 구별하다 means to distinguish, differentiate, or tell apart two or more things by their differences (區 'divide/section' + 別 'separate/distinguish', literally 'to separate into distinct parts'). As a 하다 verb it contracts to 구별해요; the items compared join with 와/과 or 하고, and the whole takes 을/를 — 진짜와 가짜를 구별하다. The crucial synonym contrast is 구별하다 vs 구분하다 (both share 區): 구별하다 stresses perceiving the DIFFERENCE between similar things ('I can't tell the twins apart' — 구별 not possible), while 구분하다 stresses SORTING items into groups/categories ('separate the trash by type' — 쓰레기를 분리수거로 구분하다). English 'distinguish' leans toward 구별하다; if you mean 'divide into sections', reach for 구분하다.

Using 구별하다 when you mean to sort items into groups — that is 구분하다; 구별하다 is for telling similar things apart.

usage: Object + 를 + 비판하다; abstract targets like 정책/결정 fit best.
The noun 비판 + 받다 = to be on the receiving end of criticism.
examples: 남을 비판하기는 쉬워요
It's easy to criticize others
비판하기 nominalizes the verb; 남(others) as the target.
언론이 그 결정을 강하게 비판했어요
The media criticized the decision harshly
결정을 강하게 비판했어요, the news-report register for public critique.
무조건 비판하지 말고 대안을 제시하세요
Don't just criticize blindly; offer an alternative
무조건 + 비판하지 말고 contrasts empty criticism with proposing solutions.
nuance: 비판하다 means to criticize — to weigh something and point out its faults through reasoned judgment, as of a policy, idea, or work (批 'judge/comment on' + 判 'judge/decide', literally 'to judge and pass verdict'). Both hanja mean 'judge', which is why proper 비판 is analytical, not just venting. As a 하다 verb it contracts to 비판해요, object 을/를. The pitfall is the near-twin pair 비판하다 vs 비난하다 (they look almost alike): 비판하다 is reasoned CRITIQUE that can be constructive ('this policy has these flaws'), while 비난하다 (難 'blame/reproach') is purely negative personal BLAME or condemnation ('you're terrible'). English 'criticize' covers both, so learners wrongly use 비판하다 for a personal attack; if you mean to blame or condemn a person, that is 비난하다.
